narrative:
The model estimates there’s a 51% chance you won’t pass your final year, which is why you’re required to take remedial courses. This isn’t a final judgment—it’s a signal that certain patterns in your situation suggest you’re at higher risk of struggling, and the extra support is meant to help you get back on track.

The biggest concern is that you’ve failed classes three times before. Students who pass their final year almost never have that many past failures, so this is the strongest warning sign. The second factor is that, unlike every other student in your group, you’ve said you don’t plan to pursue higher education. That lack of long-term academic motivation can make day-to-day effort feel less urgent. On a more positive note, having someone other than your mother or father as your main guardian actually works slightly in your favor, though it doesn’t outweigh the other two concerns.

Other parts of your background also play a role. Your parents live apart, and both have only primary-school education, which is much less common among students who pass. Neither parent works outside the home, and you chose this school mainly because of the course offering rather than its reputation or location. You don’t have internet at home, and you spend a lot of free time going out with friends and on weekends. While none of these alone would trigger the decision, together they create a picture of an uphill climb.

The good news is that the remedial courses are designed to address exactly these challenges. They’ll give you structured study time, one-on-one attention, and clearer goals. Use this opportunity to rebuild confidence, especially in subjects you’ve struggled with before, and to reconnect with your motivation for school. Small, consistent steps now can change the outcome.
